Chapter 3: The Turning Point—Facing the Roots of Anger and Pride.
Days go by, and the man finds himself stuck in the same old cycle. He wants to do better, but no matter how hard he tries, that urge to blame and criticize just won’t let up. You know how easy it is to zero in on someone else’s faults—especially when it means you don’t have to look too closely at your own.
But then, something shifts. One day, he’s sitting in a quiet room with a wise family member. He pours out all his frustrations, half-hoping for sympathy, maybe even a little backup. Instead, he gets something completely unexpected—a gentle but honest question: “What if the real problem isn’t what your spouse has done, but how you’re seeing the situation?”
That question stings a bit. Honestly, it feels unfair. He’s the one who’s been hurt, right? But as the conversation unfolds, the man starts to hear something new. His older relative shares a story from his own life, recalling a time when he also felt deeply wronged by someone close to him.
He talks about how his anger started small, but over time, it fed on every little slight and disappointment. Before long, his anger was a wall—shutting out any real connection.
Here’s the twist: Things only began to change when he let go of the need to be right. He realized that holding onto resentment wasn’t punishing the other person—it was just making him miserable. The real turning point? Choosing forgiveness. Not because the other person had earned it, but because he desperately needed peace.
That story hits home. The man sees his own life reflected right there. His anger—justified or not—has become a kind of prison, coloring every conversation, every look. He’s been so focused on his spouse’s faults, he’s lost sight of his own part in the conflict.
And honestly, most of us fall into this trap. We wait for others to change, thinking that’s when we’ll finally feel peace. But what if healing actually starts inside us? Pride and self-justification just keep the pain going, locking us into the same arguments over and over.
The man begins to understand: Forgiveness isn’t about pretending nothing happened, or letting bad behavior slide. It’s about letting go of anger’s grip and choosing a new direction. That doesn’t mean ignoring your own pain or allowing someone to mistreat you. It means refusing to let resentment define your relationship.
As these insights sink in, he feels something he hasn’t felt in a long time—relief. For the first time in months, there’s a spark of hope. Maybe he doesn’t have to wait for his spouse to change. Maybe, just maybe, he can find peace even while life is still messy.
